answers.explanation: UDP just sends. TCP sets up a connection first.
Four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length, checksum.
The client says SYN, the server answers SYN/ACK, the client confirms with ACK.
Sequence numbers and acknowledgments make that possible, at the cost of more overhead.
Retransmitting a late frame would only add delay. UDP's best effort suits live, data-rich traffic.
Five 32-bit rows: 20 bytes, before any options.
Every byte is numbered, so out-of-order segments can be slotted into place.
UDP is stateless: it remembers nothing, and resends nothing.
Like a street address (the IP) plus an apartment number (the port).
DHCP's short messages use UDP ports 67 and 68. The others need every byte, so they use TCP.
